steps.say: You doubled the side (3 to 6) but the turf did not double: it went from 9 to 36, four times as much. Doubling a side multiplies the area by 2 × 2 = 4. That is a square relationship.

You have been using area = side², a square proportion \(A \propto \text{side}^2\). Algebra writes it \(y = kx^2\): y is the area, x is the side, and k is a fixed multiplier (here k = 1). Find k from one known pair, then the equation handles every other value. The same recipe works for cubes \(x^3\), roots \(\sqrt{x}\) and inverses \(\frac{1}{x^2}\).

A square lawn 3 m on each side needs 9 m² of turf.
You want a bigger square lawn, 6 m on each side.

steps: Write the proportion as an equation with a constant k, e.g. y = kx², y = k√x or y = k/x².
Substitute the known pair and solve for k (square or root the x value first).
Put k back for the full equation, then substitute the new value to find y.
To find x from y, undo each step in turn and finish with a root. Always check.
method_card.title: Proportion with Powers
method_card.content:
At higher tier \(y\) can be proportional to a power of \(x\): \(y \propto x^2\), \(y \propto x^3\), \(y \propto \sqrt{x}\), or an inverse such as \(y \propto \frac{1}{x^2}\).

Each becomes an equation with a constant \(k\). Find \(k\) from one known pair, then the equation gives every other value. Going backwards from \(y\) to \(x\) means undoing the power last, with a root.
method_card.example:
\(y\) is proportional to \(x^2\). When \(x = 3\), \(y = 36\). Find \(y\) when \(x = 5\).

\(y = kx^2\). \(36 = k \times 9\), so \(k = 4\).

\(y = 4 \times 25 = 100\).

steps: Gold mixes inverse squares \(y = \frac{k}{x^2}\), cubes \(y = kx^3\) and inverse roots \(y = \frac{k}{\sqrt{x}}\), sometimes dressed as a real formula such as a surface area or a pendulum.
The method never changes: find \(k\) from the known pair, then substitute. Working backwards needs a cube root or a square, applied last.
Spot which quantity plays the part of \(y\) and which plays \(x\), follow the same three steps, and check in the original.
gold.title: Gold: multi-step powers and real contexts

example.question: y ∝ 1/x². When x = 3, y = 4. Find y when x = 6.

steps: Change the proportion into an equation with a multiplier \(k\): \(y \propto x^2\) becomes \(y = kx^2\), and \(y \propto \sqrt{x}\) becomes \(y = k\sqrt{x}\).
Put in the pair you are given and solve for \(k\) in one step. Square or root the \(x\) value first, then divide.
With \(k\) known the equation is complete: substitute the new value to read off \(y\), and check it reproduces the pair you started with.
bronze.title: Bronze: find k, then substitute

example.question: y ∝ x². When x = 2, y = 12. Find k.

steps: Same start: write \(y = kx^2\), \(y = k\sqrt{x}\), \(y = \frac{k}{x}\) or \(y = \frac{k}{x^2}\), then find \(k\) from the known pair.
To find \(y\), substitute the new \(x\). To find \(x\), put in the known \(y\), divide by \(k\), then take the square root last.
That final root is the step students forget. Always check your answer back in the original equation.
silver.title: Silver: roots, inverses and working backwards

example.question: y ∝ √x. When x = 25, y = 15. Find y when x = 64.

gold.hint: Multiply y by x squared to get k, then divide by the new x squared.

guided_steps.say: Inverse square: \(y = \frac{k}{x^2}\), so k = y × x². Square the known x.
So the constant is k.
guided_steps.hint: Multiply y by the squared value.

guided_steps.say: The rule is y = 36 ÷ x². New x = 6, squared.

guided_steps.done: That returns k = 36, so y = 1 is right.
guided_steps.hint: y times x squared returns k.

misconceptions.note: Student uses 1/x instead of 1/x squared: k = 4 x 3 = 12, y = 12/6 = 2.
misconceptions.message: Using \(\frac{1}{x}\) gives k = 12 and 12 ÷ 6 = 2, but this is an inverse square. k = 4 × 9 = 36, so \(y = 36 \div 36 = 1\).

gold.hint: Cube the x to find k, divide y by k, then take the cube root.

guided_steps.say: First find k. \(y = kx^3\). Cube the known x.

guided_steps.hint: Divide y by the cubed value.

guided_steps.say: The rule is y = 3x³. Now y = 192, so 192 = 3x³. Undo the 3.

guided_steps.pre: So x³ = 64. Take the cube root: x =

guided_steps.done: That gives back y = 192, so x = 4 is right.

misconceptions.note: Student stops at x cubed = 64 and gives 64 (forgets the cube root).
misconceptions.message: \(x^3 = 64\) is not x. Take the cube root: \(x = \sqrt[3]{64} = 4\).

gold.hint: Find k as a multiple of π, then multiply by the new radius squared.
gold.display: The surface area \(A\) of a sphere is proportional to \(r^2\). When \(r = 3\), \(A = 36\pi\). Find \(A\) when \(r = 5\).

misconceptions.note: Most natural numeric error (k = 36pi/3 = 12pi, A = 60pi) matches no option, so no determinate wrong option exists.
misconceptions.message: Find k from the known pair: k = 36π ÷ 3² = 4π. Then \(A = 4\pi \times 5^2 = 100\pi\). Using \(A = \pi r^2\) with no constant would give 25π, which ignores the given pair.

gold.hint: Square-root L to find k, divide T by k, then square the result for L.

guided_steps.say: First find k. \(T = k\sqrt{L}\). Square-root the known L.
The rule is T = 0.6√L. Now T = 3, so 3 = 0.6√L. Undo the 0.6.

guided_steps.done: That gives back T = 3, so L = 25 is right.

misconceptions.note: Student stops at root L = 5 and gives L = 5 (forgets to square).
misconceptions.message: \(\sqrt{L} = 5\) is only the root of L. Square it to get L itself: \(L = 5^2 = 25\).

gold.hint: Multiply y by the square root of x to get k, then divide by the new root.

guided_steps.say: Inverse root: \(y = \frac{k}{\sqrt{x}}\), so k = y × √x. Square-root the known x.
So the constant is k.
The rule is y = 12 ÷ √x. New x = 36.

guided_steps.done: That returns k = 12, so y = 2 is right.
guided_steps.hint: y times the root returns k.

misconceptions.note: Student uses x instead of root x: k = 4 x 9 = 36, y = 36/36 = 1.
misconceptions.message: Using x instead of \(\sqrt{x}\) gives k = 4 × 9 = 36 and 36 ÷ 36 = 1. Root it: k = 4 × 3 = 12, so \(y = 12 \div 6 = 2\).

bronze.hint: Square the x value, then divide y by it to get k.

guided_steps.say: Turn the proportion into an equation. \(y \propto x^2\) means \(y = kx^2\), where \(k\) is a fixed multiplier we must find.

guided_steps.hint: Divide y by the squared value.

guided_steps.done: That gives back y = 12, so k = 3 is right.

misconceptions.note: Student treats as y = kx (direct, not squared): k = 12 / 2 = 6.
misconceptions.message: Dividing y by x gives 12 ÷ 2 = 6, but the rule is \(y = kx^2\), not \(y = kx\). Divide by x squared instead: 12 ÷ 4 = 3.

bronze.hint: Square the x first, then multiply by 5.

guided_steps.say: The rule is already complete: \(y = 5x^2\). Put x = 3 in, and square the x first.
Now multiply by 5.

guided_steps.done: That returns the coefficient 5, so y = 45 is right.
guided_steps.hint: Undo the multiply to make sure.

misconceptions.note: Student computes 5 × 3 = 15 (forgets to square x first).
misconceptions.message: 5 × 3 = 15 skips the square. In \(y = 5x^2\) you square the x first: \(3^2 = 9\), then 5 × 9 = 45.

bronze.hint: Cube the x (x times x times x), then multiply by 2.

guided_steps.say: The rule is \(y = 2x^3\). Cube the x first: that is x × x × x.
Now multiply by 2.

guided_steps.done: That returns the coefficient 2, so y = 54 is right.

misconceptions.note: Student uses x squared instead of x cubed: 2 × 9 = 18.
misconceptions.message: Squaring gives \(3^2 = 9\) and 2 × 9 = 18, but this is \(x^3\). Cube the x: \(3^3 = 27\), then 2 × 27 = 54.

bronze.hint: Square-root the x value, then divide y by it to get k.

guided_steps.say: Turn the proportion into an equation. \(y \propto \sqrt{x}\) means \(y = k\sqrt{x}\).

guided_steps.hint: Divide y by the square root.

guided_steps.done: That returns y = 20, so k = 5 is right.

misconceptions.note: Student treats as y = kx: k = 20 / 16 = 1.25.
misconceptions.message: Dividing y by x gives 20 ÷ 16 = 1.25, but the rule is \(y = k\sqrt{x}\). Divide by the square root instead: 20 ÷ 4 = 5.

bronze.hint: Square-root the x first, then multiply by 4.

guided_steps.say: The rule is \(y = 4\sqrt{x}\). Square-root the x first.
Now multiply by 4.

guided_steps.done: That returns √9 = 3, so y = 12 is right.

misconceptions.note: Student forgets the root and computes 4 × 9 = 36.
misconceptions.message: 4 × 9 = 36 uses x itself, but the rule is \(y = 4\sqrt{x}\). Root the x first: \(\sqrt{9} = 3\), then 4 × 3 = 12.

guided_steps.say: This is inverse proportion: \(y = \frac{48}{x}\). The constant 48 is the product x × y and never changes.

guided_steps.pre: Write down the fixed constant. Here it is given as k =
guided_steps.hint: It is the number on top of the fraction.

guided_steps.say: Now divide the constant by the new x.

guided_steps.done: That returns k = 48, so y = 8 is right.

misconceptions.note: Student multiplies instead of divides: 48 × 6 = 288.
misconceptions.message: 48 × 6 = 288 multiplies when you should divide. \(y = \frac{48}{x}\) means 48 ÷ 6 = 8.

bronze.hint: Divide y by 7, then square-root to get x.

guided_steps.say: The rule is \(y = 7x^2\) and we know y = 112. Undo the 7 first.

guided_steps.pre: So x² = 16. Take the square root: x = √16 =
guided_steps.say: Now undo the square by rooting.

guided_steps.done: That gives back y = 112, so x = 4 is right.

misconceptions.note: Student stops at x squared = 16 and gives 16 (forgets to square root).
misconceptions.message: \(x^2 = 16\) is only halfway. You still need x, so take the square root: \(\sqrt{16} = 4\).

bronze.hint: Find k by dividing y by x squared, then use k with the new x squared.

guided_steps.say: First find k. \(y \propto x^2\) means \(y = kx^2\). Square the known x.

guided_steps.hint: Divide y by the squared value.

guided_steps.say: The rule is y = 6x². Now use the new x = 4, squared.

guided_steps.pre: Check the rule on the first pair: 6 × 1² =
guided_steps.done: That matches the given y = 6, so k = 6 is correct and y = 96 stands.

misconceptions.note: Student scales linearly: 6 × 4 = 24 (ignores squaring).
misconceptions.message: The x went up 4 times, but y does not scale the same way in a square law. \(k = 6\), so \(y = 6 \times 4^2 = 6 \times 16 = 96\), not 6 × 4 = 24.

silver.hint: Find k first, then multiply k by the new x squared.

guided_steps.say: First find k. \(y \propto x^2\) means \(y = kx^2\). Square the known x.

guided_steps.hint: Divide y by the squared value.

guided_steps.say: The rule is y = 3x². Now use the new x = 7, squared.

guided_steps.pre: Check the rule on the first pair: 3 × 3² =
guided_steps.done: That matches the given y = 27, so k = 3 is correct and y = 147 stands.

misconceptions.note: Student scales linearly (treats as direct proportion): 27 x 7/3 = 63.
misconceptions.message: Scaling y in the same ratio as x gives \(27 \times \frac{7}{3} = 63\), but \(y \propto x^2\). Find k = 3, then \(y = 3 \times 7^2 = 147\).

silver.hint: Find k by dividing y by the square root of x, then use the new x.

guided_steps.say: First find k. \(y = k\sqrt{x}\). Square-root the known x.
The rule is y = 3√x. New x = 64.

guided_steps.done: That matches the given y = 15, so y = 24 stands.

misconceptions.note: Student treats as direct proportion: k = 15/25 = 0.6, y = 0.6 x 64 = 38.4.
misconceptions.message: Treating it as \(y \propto x\) gives k = 0.6 and 0.6 × 64 = 38.4. It is a square-root law: k = 15 ÷ 5 = 3, so \(y = 3 \times 8 = 24\).

silver.hint: Multiply x and y to get k, then divide k by the new x.

guided_steps.say: Inverse proportion: \(y = \frac{k}{x}\), so k = x × y. Find k from the known pair.
The rule is y = 40 ÷ x. New x = 8.

guided_steps.done: That returns k = 40, so y = 5 is right.

misconceptions.note: Student treats as direct proportion: k = 10/4 = 2.5, y = 2.5 x 8 = 20.
misconceptions.message: Direct proportion would give k = 2.5 and 2.5 × 8 = 20, but this is inverse. Use k = x × y = 40, so \(y = 40 \div 8 = 5\).

silver.hint: Find k, divide y by k, then square-root for x.

guided_steps.say: First find k. \(y = kx^2\). Square the known x.

guided_steps.hint: Divide y by the squared value.

guided_steps.say: The rule is y = 3x². Now y = 108, so 108 = 3x². Undo the 3.

guided_steps.done: That gives back y = 108, so x = 6 is right.

misconceptions.note: Student stops at x squared = 36 and gives 36 (forgets to square root).
misconceptions.message: \(x^2 = 36\) is not the answer. Square-root it: \(x = \sqrt{36} = 6\).

silver.hint: Cube the x to find k, then use k with the new x cubed.

guided_steps.say: Cube proportion: \(y = kx^3\). Cube the known x.

guided_steps.hint: Divide y by the cubed value.

guided_steps.say: The rule is y = 5x³. New x = 3, cubed.

guided_steps.done: That matches the given y = 40, so y = 135 stands.

misconceptions.note: Student uses x squared instead of x cubed: k = 40/4 = 10, y = 10 x 9 = 90.
misconceptions.message: Using \(x^2\) gives k = 10 and 10 × 9 = 90, but the power is 3. Cube it: k = 40 ÷ 8 = 5, so \(y = 5 \times 27 = 135\).

silver.hint: Multiply y by x squared to get k, then divide k by the new x squared.

guided_steps.say: Inverse square: \(y = \frac{k}{x^2}\), so k = y × x². Square the known x.
So the constant is k.
guided_steps.hint: Multiply y by the squared value.

guided_steps.say: The rule is y = 20 ÷ x². New x = 5, squared.

guided_steps.done: That returns k = 20, so y = 0.8 is right.
guided_steps.hint: y times x squared returns k.

misconceptions.note: Student uses 1/x instead of 1/x squared: k = 5 x 2 = 10, y = 10/5 = 2.
misconceptions.message: Using \(\frac{1}{x}\) gives k = 10 and 10 ÷ 5 = 2. It is an inverse square: k = 5 × 4 = 20, so \(y = 20 \div 25 = 0.8\).

silver.hint: Find k, divide y by k to get the root, then square it for x.

guided_steps.say: First find k. \(y = k\sqrt{x}\). Square-root the known x.
The rule is y = 5√x. Now y = 25, so 25 = 5√x. Undo the 5.

guided_steps.done: That gives back y = 25, so x = 25 is right.

misconceptions.note: Student stops at root x = 5 and gives x = 5 (forgets to square).
misconceptions.message: \(\sqrt{x} = 5\) is only halfway. Square both sides to get x: \(x = 5^2 = 25\).

problem_bank.bronze_description: Find the constant k in one step, or substitute straight into a completed rule.
